lines.note: Continues the preceding entry with the intended sense of consideration; samazamani seken wo begins an example about examining the world in different ways. The scan appears to print anomalous ſileração rather than expected ſideração: comparison with Conſiderar below leaves no secure bowl on the third letter, so the supplied literal reading is retained with this caveat.
Ukagai miru completes the example of observing or considering the world. Portuguese mui- continues as tas on the next physical row.
Completes muitas maneiras, 'in many ways', then adds the sense of looking for something by sight. The initial t in tas corrects OCR eas.
Ukame is referred to ukabe, 'float or cause to float'. This is a new entry aligned with the other headwords, so the draft's indentation is removed.
Ukami is referred to ukabi; the abbreviation bu supplies the dictionary form ukabu. The upright b and u replace the OCR's mixed-font hu.
Ukarakashi, ukarakasu, ukarakaita means exciting or stirring someone. The historical principal part aita remains as printed.

runs.text: aluoroçar a alguem de maneira que fique como

lines.note: Continues the definition: stirring someone in such a manner that the person becomes absorbed or suspended in attention. Aluoroçar retains the historical spelling.
The person is carried away or absorbed; kokoro wo u- starts the example continued below. Vt introduces the example in the italic apparatus.
The divided ukarakasu completes kokoro wo ukarakasu, exciting the heart. The Portuguese manner phrase is itself divided across the row boundary.

runs.text: ra o coração, ou vontade. ¶ Item, Pro-

lines.note: Completes maneira and identifies the heart or will as the affected object. A new sense starts with Pro-, continued as uocar below.

runs.text: uocar aſi, ou a outro ao vicio da ſenſualida-

lines.note: The second sense is inciting oneself or another to sensual vice. The physical division of sensualida-de is retained.
Irogonomi ni hito no kokoro wo begins the example of stirring another person's heart toward sensual desire. The final u- belongs with karakasu on the next row.
Ukarakasu completes the example, and the Portuguese begins 'provoke and move someone toward' the sensuality named below.

After the translation's sensualidade, irogonomi ni ukarakasa- begins the passive example. The scan supports contiguous Irogonomini and initial v, correcting the OCR's separated Iro gonomini and xcaraca-.
Saruru completes ukarakasaruru, a historical passive form: to be moved or carried away. The Portuguese continues the description of absorption below.
Completes the passive gloss as being swept away by sensuality. This short continuation closes ukarakasu before the next entry.
Ukare, ukaruru, ukareta describes being alert, stirred, or absorbed. The principal form uru is retained rather than modernized to a modern conjugation.
The example describes the heart being captivated on seeing a dance. The unusual printed n in Vondoriuo is retained rather than silently regularized; the Portuguese begins Vẽ-do across the line break.

runs.text: do algũa dança eſtar muito atẽto, & como en-

lines.note: Completes vendo and describes watching a dance intently. The nasal abbreviation in atẽto and the division en-leuado remain literal.

runs.text: leuado com goſto. ¶ Item, Eſtar prouoca-

lines.note: Completes enleuado com gosto, being pleasantly absorbed. The second sense begins being provoked or stirred toward sensuality.
Completes the sensuality sense of ukare. This is a continuation of the preceding entry, not another headword.

runs.text: Andar de cà pera là como

lines.note: Ukarearuki means wandering here and there in an absorbed or distracted state. The Portuguese de cà pera là expresses that roaming movement.

runs.text: ſuſpenſo buſcando algũa couſa, ou como enle-

lines.note: Explains wandering as if searching for something while distracted. The visible u supports buscando, correcting OCR bascando.

runs.text: uado, & ſuſpenſo com amores, ou ſaudades.

lines.note: Completes the explanation with absorption in love or longing. Saudades retains the historical emotional nuance rather than a simple physical search.

Ukareme is identified as a poetic equivalent of yuujo. The Portuguese describes a lascivious or public woman; visible r corrects the malformed OCR Vcateme. The lightly slanted P is retained as the draft's italic usage label, although its isolated typeface is less secure than the adjacent words.

runs.text: ou publica, que tem por officio cantar, & bai-

lines.note: Continues the definition as a woman whose profession includes singing and dancing. The line ends with the first part of bai-lar.

runs.text: lar, & dar paßa tempo a outros.

lines.note: Completes bailar and adds entertaining other people. The printed separated paßa tempo is retained.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de estar ſuſpenſo ſem

lines.note: Ukkarito describes being distracted or inattentive. The two c letters support Vccarito rather than OCR Vecarito.
Completes sem aduertir and gives ukkarito shita mono, a distracted person. Portuguese Peſ- is divided before ſoa on the next row.

runs.text: ſoa que està como eſtupida, ou enleuada em al-

lines.note: Completes the description as a person who is stupefied or absorbed in something. The Portuguese algũa is divided al-gũa across the physical rows.
Gũa couſa completes the preceding algũa couſa. The brief continuation belongs to the distracted-person example.
Ukaukato is an adverb for being absent-minded or suspended in attention. The repetition in the Japanese is preserved as the printed headword.
Adds being as if alienated or mentally elsewhere, completing the adverbial definition.
Ukaukashii means light-minded or lacking judgment, as expressed by leue and de pouca cabeça.
Ukaukashisa is the corresponding quality noun, carrying forward the preceding light-mindedness definition without a repeated Portuguese gloss.
Ukaukashuu is the adverbial form, explicitly labelled Adu. The caron on final u is retained.
Ukashi, ukasu, ukaita means making something float; Meliùs recommends ukabe as the preferable form. The final Fa- starts the Portuguese infinitive fazer.

runs.text: zer nadar, ou estar ſobre a agoa. Vt,

lines.note: Completes fazer nadar, or keeping something upon the water. Fu- begins fune in the example on the next row.
Fune wo ukasu means making a boat float. The short row completes the divided Japanese example.
Uchi is explained by chiye ari, having knowledge. The following example contrasts people with knowledge and those without it.

runs.text: Os que tem, & os que não

lines.note: Muchi no mono completes the contrast between people who have knowledge and those who do not. The Portuguese mirrors that paired construction.
Tem ſaber completes the negative clause for those without knowledge. The short row closes this sense of uchi.
Uchi here means inside or during a period. Ie no begins the first example, referring to the inside of a house.
Ie no uchi is inside the house; mairanu uchi begins the temporal example, while one has not gone. These are distinct uses of the same printed headword.
Ni completes mairanu uchi ni. Portuguese Em quanto não vou supplies the temporal meaning; the visible m corrects OCR Ens.
Uchi denotes falcon droppings. Uchi wo tsuku begins the example; the dot-like mark after tçu is retained at the physical division before qu.

runs.text: Botarem os falcões o eſterco, ou excre-

lines.note: Qu completes tsuku, and the Portuguese explains falcons voiding droppings or excrement. The faint word falcões is supported by its surviving f, l, nasal vowel and the identical subject in the preceding definition; OCR ſal des is spurious.
Mentos completes excrementos, closing the falcon-droppings entry and the left column.
Uchi, utsu, utta introduces the broad verb meaning strike or give blows. The abbreviated principal parts retain the printed initial v.
Kao wo utsu means slapping the face. Te- begins teki in the next example.
Teki wo utsu means striking or defeating enemies; the Portuguese explicitly includes killing them. The physical Te-qiuo division is preserved.
Tsuzumi wo utsu is playing a drum. The Portuguese description begins with sounding a certain instrument, completed below.
Tabaquinho supplies the small-drum gloss; bakuchi wo utsu then begins the gambling example. The historical word and spelling are retained.
Completes the gambling gloss as playing dice. Kane wo utsu introduces an oath-taking usage, whose Portuguese translation continues below.

runs.text: to juramento batendo com hum ferro noutro.

lines.note: Explains the oath as striking one piece of iron against another. This specifies the special sense of kane wo utsu rather than ordinary bell ringing.
Go wo utsu is playing go. The Portuguese begins an explanation of the game by reference to its many small stones.
Completes the game description and starts hito wo utsu, striking a person. Eſpã- continues as car on the next row.
Completes the gloss as beating or killing someone, then starts mizu wo utsu. A visible space separates matar a, correcting OCR matara.

runs.text: Botar agoa com a mão, ou

lines.note: Mizu wo utsu is equated with sosoku and explained as casting water with the hand. The Japanese explanatory synonym remains a separate roman span.

runs.text: agoar. ¶ Item, Fazer certas obras de

lines.note: Agoar completes the water-sprinkling sense. The entry then extends utsu to making certain kinds of handiwork.
Uma no kura wo utsu exemplifies the craft sense by making a horse saddle. The object noun kura is not a blow directed at the animal.
Completes the saddle gloss, then gives yumi wo utsu, making a bow. Its Portuguese object continues below.
Completes the bow-making gloss and gives yumi uchi as the bow maker. The scan has capital Y in Yumi and a single final l in Official, correcting OCR vumi and Officiall.
De arcos completes the bow-maker description; mushiro wo utsu begins the example of making mats.
Esteiras completes the mat-making gloss. O wo utsu introduces cord or braid making, explained on the following row.
The cords or braid complete the preceding example. Katana wo u- begins the sword-making example continued below.
Completes katana wo utsu as making swords, then gives ta wo utsu for working a field. The printed La has no supplied terminal hyphen before urar below.
Completes laurar as ploughing or digging low-lying fields. Kirimu- begins kirimugi in the following example.
Kirimugi wo utsu describes making wheat noodles, rendered a letria de trigo. The printed word spacing is retained.
Hi wo utsu means striking fire. Tori- begins the example of catching birds on the next row.

runs.text: Tomar com rede marrecas que ſe

lines.note: Tori wo utsu is explained as catching ducks or teal in a net. The relative clause describes the birds' movement below.
The birds rise from the ground and fly; tori- then starts the compound toriuchi naming a catching place.

runs.text: Lugar onde tomão eſtas marrecas com

lines.note: Toriuchi is a place where these ducks are caught. The definition continues with the means of catching them.

runs.text: rede que ſe lhes lança em cima. ¶

lines.note: The net is thrown over the birds. Hato wo begins the following example concerning pigeons.

runs.text: Tomar pombas com rede de tombo.

lines.note: Hato wo utsu is catching pigeons with a falling or overturning net. The Portuguese rede de tombo specifies the mechanism.

runs.text: Rede de tombo de tomar paſ

lines.note: Uchiami names such a cast or falling net. The printed paſ ends without an added hyphen before ſaros on the next physical row.

runs.text: ſaros, ou rede como tarrafa pera tomar peixe.

lines.note: Completes paſſaros and extends the net definition to a cast net for fish. The shared net mechanism links the bird-catching and fishing senses.
Tsuru wo utsu means plucking or touching a bowstring. The Portuguese explains how its sound is tested below.

runs.text: puxando por ella pera ver ſe ſoa bem. Item,

lines.note: The string is pulled to determine whether it sounds well. Item begins a figurative extension of this testing action.

runs.text: per met. Ver, & palpar algũa couſa que hum

lines.note: The figurative sense is looking at and feeling something in order to learn about it. The abbreviation per met. is retained without expansion.

runs.text: quer ſaber, &c. ¶ Este verbo ſe ajunta, & cõ-

lines.note: Completes the wish to know about the object. The lexicographic comment then says this verb joins and compounds with many others.

runs.text: poem com muitos outros. Algũas vezes dà

lines.note: Completes compoem and introduces the effects that utsu can have in compounds. The divided cõ-poem remains literal.

runs.text: mais força, & enfaſi: & outras no mais que

lines.note: Sometimes the compound adds force or emphasis; sometimes it adds no more than elegance. The printed no is retained rather than silently normalized to não.

runs.text: elegancia, como ſe verà a baixo.

lines.note: Completes the grammatical comment by directing the reader to the following entries for examples of that elegance.
Uchiage, uchiaguru, uchiageta means throwing upward. The following example illustrates throwing a stone high.
Tsubute wo uchiaguru is throwing stones upward. The Portuguese pe- begins pedradas on the next line.

runs.text: dradas. ¶ Item, Dar a embarcação à costa.

lines.note: Completes pedradas, then adds the sense of a vessel coming ashore. The explanation turns from throwing upward to grounding a boat.
Fune wo uchiageta is illustrated by a boat running aground. Fune reappears inside the Portuguese translation as the Japanese word for boat; it is eligible for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: as ondas derão com a Fune à costa. ¶

lines.note: Explains that the waves drove the boat onto the shore. Fune is again embedded in Portuguese, while Co- begins koe in a new Japanese example.
Koe wo uchiagete utoo means singing with the voice raised. The caron in vtǒ is visible and retained.
Completes the translation as raising the voice high. The visible t in alto corrects OCR alio.
Uchiai and its listed principal forms mean meeting or coming into contact with something. The scan supports Vchiai and final a in couſa, correcting OCR Vehiai and couſo.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Darſe de pancadas, ou cutiladas hũ

lines.note: Adds the reciprocal sense of exchanging blows or sword cuts. The visible t supports cutiladas rather than OCR cuiladas.
Ao outro completes the reciprocal phrase, one against the other. It closes uchiau before the next entry.
Uchiake, uchiakuru, uchiaketa means opening completely. Itẽ introduces a further sense that continues on the next page; Deſpejar below is the catchword, not another body line.
The first signature letter is abraded; its surviving upper strokes support capital Y, followed by two clear lowercase y letters and the numeral 2.
